source.title: Guiding Through Complexity: What Makes Good Supervision for Hard Reasoning Tasks?
source.authors: Xuan He; Da Yin; Nan-Yun Peng

page_placements.theme: Weak-label quality and predictors of W2S outcome (self-consistency, sample reward, step-error severity, supervisor variance, error similarity, intrinsic dimension)
Easy-to-hard generalization (training on easy or decomposed tasks, or with easy-trained reward models, tested on hard ones)

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure labels are garbled in the text extraction, but the relevant prose and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It empirically tests how supervision quality and source relate to fine-tuning performance, but uses a different setup and does not calculate PGR or compare student performance directly with supervisor performance.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SFT results using synthetic noisy full-task and subtask labels, plus results using solutions sampled from several teacher models. It does not report PGR or teacher-versus-student performance comparisons. Figure 2’s plotted point values are not transcribed where the text does not state them. Table 2’s combined-supervision results compare data strategies, not the claim’s PGR measure.
record.test_reason: The paper sits in the weak-to-strong literature but never measures the weak-to-strong effect. It fine-tunes one Llama-3-8B student on synthetically noised or teacher-sampled math solutions and compares accuracy across supervision recipes. There is no supervisor-versus-student comparison, no strong ceiling, and no PGR. The 'weak' teachers (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, GPT-3.5-turbo, Command-R) are mostly stronger than the 8B student. Outcome error rates are set by swapping in wrong solutions, not by a weaker model's capability. What it studies is label-noise robustness and supervision-strategy choice, a related but different construct. Its findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude three things. Hard-task supervision, even at high outcome error rates, beats correct subtask supervision. Step-wise error rate matters more than outcome error rate. Combining hard and subtask supervision beats doubled epochs or rephrased data. They draw no conclusion about PGR or about students exceeding weak supervisors.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Llama-3-8B SFT and compares synthetic noisy hard-task labels with decomposed subtask labels; it does not reproduce the original weak-to-strong setup or calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with supervision type, teacher model, outcome error rate, benchmark, and step-wise error rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-3-8B SFT on hard-task math solutions with up to 90% wrong final answers beats SFT on fully correct subtask solutions. On MATH, hard supervision at 90% error beats subtask supervision at 10% error by about 11% (16.9% on Gaokao-Mathcloze). Accuracy changes little across 0-100% outcome error rates for hard supervision.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on hard-task reasoning traces is robust to wrong final answers, and beats correct easier-subtask supervision, for hard math benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: At similar outcome error rates, a teacher's step-wise error rate tracks student accuracy. Command-R-2024-08 supervision (87.7% error) gives 32.8% on MATH versus 44.8% for GPT-4o-mini (90% error). In Table 3, combined supervision from the highest step-error teacher (Command-R-2024-03) gives the lowest accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The severity of reasoning-step errors in teacher-generated supervision predicts student performance better than the final-answer error rate does.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding the corresponding subtask supervision to hard-task supervision raises accuracy on most of the five benchmarks. It also beats doubling the epochs or merging rephrased data (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Augmenting hard-task supervision with decomposed-subtask supervision improves fine-tuning on hard math.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No PGR is reported and no weak-teacher versus fine-tuned-student performance comparison is made. The main model comparison uses a single 8B student and math tasks only. Some results are given only in figures; uncertainty estimates are not reported. Step-wise error rates are based on human review of 60 sampled incorrect solutions.
record.rows_left_out: Individual Figure 2 benchmark accuracies across the full 0%-100% error-rate sweep and individual Figure 3 benchmark values are not extracted where the text gives no readable values. Other Table 2 combinations and doubled-epoch/rephrased-data comparisons are not included because they are accuracy comparisons between supervision recipes, not PGR results. Table 3 combination results are likewise omitted.

untested.parts: Entirely untested: no student-versus-supervisor comparison, no strong ceiling, no PGR.
Untested: no auxiliary confidence loss, no ensembling, no loss variants, no PGR.
Untested: no sweep of supervisor or student size, no PGR. Varies only supervision noise and source for one 8B student on math.
Untested: no exploitation of the supervisor, no distribution shift, no error-similarity analysis.
Untested: no vision or other non-language modality.

missing.what: Table 3: combined supervision from different teachers (GPT-4o-mini 46.8, Llama-3-70B 31.2, Command-R-2024-03 24.6 on MATH). This bears only on the fits_no_version finding about step-wise errors, not on any version.
Headline gaps between hard and subtask supervision (about 11% on MATH, 16.9% on Gaokao-Mathcloze at 90% vs 10% error). These bear only on the fits_no_version finding.

record.verdict_notes: Every version is set to none: the study never compares the student with its supervisor or a strong ceiling. The teachers are mostly stronger than the 8B student, so the 'weak' framing is nominal. The 'weak' labels come from synthetic noise injection, built by swapping in wrong solutions mainly sampled from GPT-4o. The reader's V3 labels are withdrawn.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare a strong student’s performance with the weak supervisor’s performance or calculate PGR.
Does not test auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants for PGR gains. Combined subtask/full-task data is reported using accuracy, not PGR.

Tests math tasks and variation across teacher-generated supervision and step-wise error rates. Does not sweep student size, test NLP, chess, or reward modelling, examine representations, or measure PGR.
Does not test distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models make similar errors.
No theoretical conditions are tested or established.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.

relation.reason: The paper discusses weak-to-strong generalization as motivation and related work, while measuring a different supervision-quality question.

tranche.reason: The experiments compare supervision difficulty, noise and sources; they do not measure students exceeding weak supervisors, PGR, or another listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is v3, dated 25 February 2025. Rows r6–r10 describe supervision quality rather than claim results; the source's conflicting teacher outcome-error rates are correctly disclosed in r11 and r13.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Teacher-generated math supervision with similar outcome error rates
reader_labels.reason: Results vary with teacher source, and the authors report that lower step-wise error rates align with higher downstream performance; see r4-r10 and r12-r13.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Controlled variation in outcome error rate on MATH and across math benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Performance is not a simple function of outcome error rate: the MATH drop differs between hard and subtask labels, and on JEE-Bench 100% error hard labels are reported better than 10%; see r1-r3.
